p: On the first Saturday in April, Graham ran Kit's first full practice test at the kitchen table, eleven blocks in the order and the minutes the real test uses. He called time at the end of every block and said nothing else all morning.

In Word Knowledge she hit the word dissemble, to put on a false front, and knew it for her own seven years. When a math problem stalled her, she guessed, marked it and moved on. In Physical Science, the subject Graham has taught for years and she'd never once asked him about, she knew from the water plant that the pressure at the bottom of a tank depends on its depth, not its width.

That night she put her 2019 score sheet on the kitchen table and told Graham herself. Her Pilot score had been nineteen. When Boyd asked her to stay for an inspection, she'd said yes, because yes meant she never had to say nineteen to Graham, and she'd let Boyd's request be the reason. Graham said he'd made his peace with the pilot slot back in January. What he couldn't get past was that she'd let him think it was Boyd for seven years. She didn't defend it. She said, I did, and stayed at the table.

Then he took her out to the garage and folded back a corner of the tarp over the crib. Two springs ago he'd asked her whether this was the year they'd try for a baby, and she'd said after. He asked her not to hand him another after. She told him she didn't know yet, that she wanted to fly, and that she wasn't going to say after to make the night easier. He said okay.

On Sunday she called her mother and asked for an hour at her table on Sunday, April 11, when drill lets out at four, to tell her something from 2019 in person. Rhonda said she'd make a roast. On Tuesday she told Vern that Graham knew, and he said, that's one. On Wednesday Graham kept the lab date he'd put on the whiteboard in February. In Room 114 he told her his sophomores bring him failing tests every week, and she could have brought him a nineteen. Then he taught her density, hydraulics and circuits, careful and kind, and he didn't say her name all afternoon.

Friday morning she came home from a night shift to her practice test scored in red. His only note said AR, twenty one of twenty five, Good. Her weakest blocks for the Pilot composite were Instrument Comprehension and Aviation Information, the airplane from the inside. She stuck his note on the fold of her 2019 sheet, so it would come out of her pocket first. Then she wrote him a note of her own and stuck it on the coffee maker. PS, thirteen of twenty. Will you teach me the seven?

Saturday, April 10, ten to four in the morning. The launch board was where it always was, on the wall by the coffee, and two two eight was on it for eight thirty. Beside it, in Boyd's grease pencil from February, DARROW. Same board as March. In March the thing that had to come off before the jet went anywhere had been a tire.
The light was on in Boyd's office. It was always on by now. She could see the top of his head over the partition and the steam off his cup.

Her note had been gone from the coffee maker when she woke up Friday afternoon. Nothing in its place. At supper Graham had told her about a kid in third period who'd wired a doorbell backward, and he'd laughed, and he hadn't said one word about the seven. She hadn't asked. It was his to answer.
The sheet was in her coat, folded, with his yellow note on the outside. She didn't take it out. Boyd wouldn't need paper. She'd ask him for ten minutes once the jet was gone.
Vern's Nav Table: Inside the Jet.
I sat sideways at a little table for twenty one years, Sergeant, and I could read the pilots' panel upside down from six feet back. You can learn it at a kitchen table.

Instrument Comprehension comes tenth. The current Pearson page gives it 25 questions in five minutes, which is twelve seconds apiece, one of the shortest clocks on the test. Each question has two dials, an attitude indicator on the left and a compass on the right, and then four little pictures of an airplane up in the sky. One of the four matches both dials. On the 2015 pamphlet it's the only block with four choices instead of five. You find the right picture by throwing out the wrong ones, one cue at a time, and I'll give you the order I'd use.

Aviation Information is dead last. Five hours in, and you're about wrung out like a dishrag by then. Twenty questions in eight minutes, 24 seconds each, five choices. It's the inside of the airplane and the ground around it. What holds a wing up, what the controls do, what the gauges read, what the paint and the lights on an airport are trying to tell you. The Pilot composite leans on both of these. So it's where a Pilot number gets made, along with the math and the tables. I'd have studied it first, if anybody had asked me in 1973. Nobody did.
How the exam asks it. Twelve seconds a picture, 24 seconds a question. Both clocks are short. You don't beat either one by staring.

It's the pilot's picture of the real horizon, for when the real one's gone. Cloud. Night. The inside of a thunderstorm over Nebraska, which I've been in, and don't recommend. There's a little airplane in the middle, stuck to the case. It never moves. Behind it the horizon moves, a line with sky on top and ground underneath. So you read it like a window. Little airplane against that line, your airplane against the world.

Pitch first. Little airplane's nose above the horizon line, your real nose is above the real horizon. Climbing. Line above the little airplane, you're diving. Line right through it, level. Where people go wrong is that the line's what moves, so in a climb the horizon slides down the face of the dial, and they see a low line and holler dive. I've watched a captain do it on a trainer in front of his whole crew, and he bought the beer.

Bank next. Roll right and the world outside tips the other way, so the horizon goes up on the right side of the dial and down on the left. Lean your head right in a car on a curve sometime and watch the fields. So look at the ends of the horizon line. Whichever end sits higher, that's the side of your low wing. Line higher on the right, right bank. Then check it with the pointer at the top. It sits off the zero mark toward the low wing, and the marks tell you how far, 10 and 20 and 30, then 45 and 60 on most of them. At twelve seconds you want which way and about how far. Nobody's grading you on the third digit.

Try one. Horizon line below the little airplane, and higher on the left side of the dial than the right. Nose above the line, climbing. Line's high on the left, so the low wing's on the left. Banked left, and the pointer's off zero to the left to agree. Climbing left turn. Say right and you read it backward, like a mirror. I did that for a month in 1974, in a trainer in a back room at Mather, and the sergeant who ran it called me Lieutenant Backward till Thanksgiving.
How the exam asks it. Horizon below the little airplane, climbing. Horizon above it, diving. The higher end of the line is the low wing, and the pointer should agree.

The compass on the right is the easy one. That's why you start there. On the test's dial the needle points at the heading, which is where the nose is pointed. North is 360, or 000. East's 090. South, 180. West, 270. Halfway between, northeast is 045, then southeast 135, southwest 225, northwest 315. We said them in three digits out loud on the airplane. Two seven zero. Zero four five. A copilot from Texas said forty five to me once and I had us halfway to Oklahoma in my head before he said he meant zero four five.

Heading's where the nose points. Not where the airplane is, and in a wind, not quite where it's going either, as you found out in March. The opposite heading is 180 off. Add 180, or take it away if you're past 180. The reverse of 070 is 250. The reverse of 300, 120. Turning right adds, turning left takes away, and either one wraps around past north. From 330, sixty to the right is 030. Not 390. There's no 390, though I knew a pilot in 1983 who'd argue it. He could do the rest of them in his head faster than me, and I never forgave him.
How the exam asks it. Compass first. It's the fastest cue on the page, and it throws out the most pictures.

Now the pictures. Every one of them's drawn for the same observer, and that's you. You're standing south of the airplane, up at its altitude, somehow, looking north at it. East is on the right. West's on the left. Get that nailed down and the rest is where the nose points.

Heading 090, east, nose to your right, and you're looking at its side. Heading 270, west, nose to the left. Heading 360, north, flying away from you, so you see the tail. Heading 180, south, coming right at you, nose toward you, and you're who it's headed for. In between, it splits the difference. 045's going away and off to your right. 225's coming at you and off to your left. A boom operator I flew with used to say every one of these is just a clock face you're standing under, and I never did figure out what he meant.

Bank's where the points go missing. Going away, north, it's easy. Its right wing's on your right, so a right bank drops the wing on your right. Coming at you, south, it's all flipped. Its right wing is over on your left, so a right bank drops the wing on your left. That one's worth slowing down for. I sat Patrice's nephew on a kitchen chair facing me with a pot lid for a steering wheel, and he had it in about four tries. Climb in the seat in your head, face the way it's facing, and ask which wing is down from in there. Side on, heading east, the right wing's the near one. Bank right, the near wing drops, the airplane tips its back toward you, and you look down on top of it. Bank left, the far wing drops, and you get the belly.

Pitch is easiest seen side on. Climbing east, the nose points up and to the right. Straight away or straight at you, it's harder. A climb going away tips the back toward you, so you look down on it. A climb coming at you shows you the belly. Patrice can't do these with a magazine in her lap. She gets up, faces north by the sink, and works it out standing. It works. I quit laughing at it years ago.
How the exam asks it. Nose toward you means its right is your left. Get in the seat before you call the bank.
You don't have to like that clock, Sergeant. You do have to quit arguing with it.

Here's the order. Compass first. Find the heading, then run your eye across the four pictures looking at noses. Toward you, away with the tail toward you, or off to a side. Any picture pointed wrong is out, and a lot of the time that's two gone in three seconds. Bank second. Which end of the horizon line is higher? That's the low wing. Cross off the pictures with the other wing down, or with none down at all. Pitch last. Climb, dive, level. By then there's usually one left standing. That's eliminating one cue at a time. You never carry all three in your head at once. Check one. Cross off. Check the next.

On our practice tests each wrong picture misses on one cue, a wrong heading, the wrong wing down, or the nose the wrong way. On the real test a wrong one can miss on two, which only makes it easier to toss. Stuck at twelve seconds between two of them? Take one and go. Nothing comes off for a wrong answer, so a guess is free, and Pearson wants every one answered anyway. Twenty five in five minutes is no place to sit on number nine and never meet number twenty. I'd rather you guess the last few on purpose than run out of clock and guess them in a hurry.

Try one in words. Horizon line below the little airplane and higher on the left, pointer off to the left, needle on 090. Compass first. East, nose to the right, so any nose pointed left or at you goes. Bank, left. Heading east, the left wing's the far one, so you want the far wing low and the belly showing. Pitch, horizon below, climbing. Nose up and to the right, far wing low, belly toward you. Three looks. You'd have had time to scratch your ear.
How the exam asks it. Heading, bank, pitch, in that order. Cross off. Guess at twelve seconds and move.

Four forces. I drew them on a napkin for every new copilot, whether they wanted it or not, and most of them didn't. Two pairs. Lift up, weight down. Thrust ahead, drag behind. Weight pulls straight at the middle of the earth from the center of gravity, and on a tanker that center wanders all morning as the fuel goes out the boom. Lift works square to the air going past. Thrust is the engines. Drag is the air, being the air.

Straight and level at a steady speed, the pairs come out even. Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, and there's nothing more to it. Folks want there to be some thrust left over, or how does it keep going? It keeps going because nothing's holding it back harder than the engines push. Push more than the drag and you speed up, or climb. Less, you slow down, or settle. We'd hand off forty thousand pounds on a long track, and coming home the pilots kept easing the throttles back a hair at a time. Lighter airplane, less lift. Half the copilots never noticed their own hands doing it, and I never told them.
How the exam asks it. Steady and level means balanced. Lift equals weight, thrust equals drag. Not more of either.

Picture a wing sawed in half crossways, and look at the cut end. That's an airfoil. Round and fat in front, the leading edge. Thin as a knife at the back, the trailing edge. On most, more curve on top. That's camber. String a line from the nose of it to the tail and you've got the chord line. The relative wind is the air the wing's flying through. It comes straight at the wing from wherever the wing's headed, the way rain hits the windshield harder the faster you drive. Level flight, it comes in level. Sinking, it comes up at you from below.

Angle of attack is the chord line against the relative wind. It isn't the wing against the ground. It isn't where the nose points, either, and that's the one they'll try on you. I've watched a tanker on approach sitting nose up and sinking seven hundred feet a minute, and the wind was coming at that wing from underneath like a fire hose. Huge angle of attack. Angle of incidence is a different animal, the angle they bolted the wing on at, chord against the fuselage. The factory sets it. I've heard pilots blame it anyhow.

Two things make the lift, both at once. Over the curved top the air speeds up. Fast air presses less. So the top gets pulled harder than the bottom gets pushed. That's Bernoulli. Hold a strip of paper under your lip and blow across the top of it, and up it comes. The wing also shoves air down off its back edge, and the air shoves back. That's Newton's third law, Graham's week. More angle of attack, more lift, up to a point. Twice the speed is four times the lift. It goes with the square. Thicker air, more lift. More wing, more lift. Hot, high and humid is thin air. July in Albuquerque with a full load, we used every foot of runway they owned and some of the dirt past it, and the boom operator prayed out loud.
How the exam asks it. Angle of attack is measured from the relative wind. A choice that measures it from the horizon has the wrong angle.

Every wing's got a critical angle of attack. On a lot of them it's somewhere around 16 to 20 degrees. Push past it and the air can't hang on to the curve over the top. It breaks off and tumbles, and the lift falls out from under you all at once. That's a stall. Engines don't come into it. Gliders stall. It's the wing. Say it twice.

So any airspeed, any attitude, any power. Slow's the common way, since slow takes a big angle of attack to hold you up. Haul back hard in a fast turn, though, and you'll stall at a speed you'd have bet the farm on. The stall speed in the book is wings level at one weight. Heavier, it goes up. Bank, it goes up, because a level turn asks the wing for more than the airplane weighs. Sixty degrees of bank and you weigh double, and the stall speed comes up about forty percent. I read that in a magazine at the barber's in 1971 and never once forgot it. Flaps bring it back down. That's why you land with them hanging out.

The fix is less angle of attack. Ease the nose down, or let off the back pressure, and the air comes back onto the top of the wing. Then power, then level the wings. The miss is hauling back to keep the nose up, the one thing that keeps it stalled, and the thing your hands want worst. Stall it with one wing worse off than the other and a little yaw, and it can wind up a spin. Fellow I knew rented a Cessna one April, took me up and spun it on purpose over a bean field outside Marshall. I've never been so glad to see Missouri the right way up.
How the exam asks it. A stall is about angle, not speed. The cure's less angle of attack, so the nose goes down, not up.

Two kinds. Parasite drag is the air shoving back on everything that isn't making lift. The shape pushing through, the skin rubbing, the seams where two parts meet and stir it up. It grows with the square of the speed. Twice as fast, four times as much. Induced drag is what lift costs you. High pressure under the wing curls around the tip toward the low pressure on top, and that spin off each wingtip tips the lift back a hair. It's worst slow, at a big angle of attack, and it eases off as you speed up.

So somewhere there's a speed where the two add up to the least. That's where the wing gets the most lift for its drag, and about where an airplane glides farthest with the engine quit. Slower, induced drag climbs. Faster, parasite climbs. It makes a U on paper. Graham would call it a parabola, and he'd be close enough for me.

Those wingtip vortices don't quit when the airplane leaves. They roll off the tips and sink, and they're strongest behind an airplane that's heavy, clean and slow, gear and flaps up, just after takeoff. Wake turbulence. We caught another tanker's wake once on a track over Kansas, and every coffee cup on our flight deck went up and came down someplace else. Down low, about a wingspan off the runway, the ground gets in the way of the vortices. Induced drag drops off and the airplane wants to float. Ground effect. It's why a hot landing just goes on and on, and the far fence keeps getting closer.
How the exam asks it. Slow and heavy is induced drag. Fast is parasite drag. They'll swap them on you.

You had the three axes in January. Ailerons roll it, elevator pitches it, rudder yaws it. Here's what comes along for the ride. Roll right and the left aileron goes down, which lifts that wing, and a wing that's lifting harder drags harder too. So for a second the nose swings left, the wrong way. Adverse yaw. A touch of right rudder squares it away, and the turn comes out clean. Coordinated, the pilots say, the way you'd say a man's sober. A few airplanes don't bother with an elevator and swing the whole horizontal tail in one piece. That's a stabilator. Corbin could tell you which ones.

Trim tabs. A little hinged strip on the back edge of a control surface. Set it and it holds the surface where the pilot wants it, so nobody has to sit holding the yoke for an hour over Iowa with both arms cramping. Trim takes the pressure off. It doesn't steer anything. Flaps, back on the inboard trailing edge, add lift and drag together, so you can come down steeper and slower. Slats, out front on the leading edge, let the wing take a bigger angle before it quits on you. Spoilers pop up off the top of the wing on the big ones and dump lift. After touchdown they put the weight on the wheels so the brakes will bite. Some jets use them in the air to help roll, or for speed brakes, and the whole airplane shakes like a wet dog.

Stability is the airplane wanting to go back where it was. The horizontal tail keeps the nose from bobbing around. The vertical fin keeps it pointed into the wind like the rooster on a barn roof out on Route 9. Wings tipped up a little from root to tip, dihedral, roll it back level on their own. Then the center of gravity. It has to sit inside its limits, usually a bit ahead of where the lift works. Too far forward, nose heavy, and you'll fight to get the nose up to land. Too far back, twitchy, and it may not come out of a stall at all. We weighed and balanced every pallet that went on that airplane. I signed every sheet, and I can still see the form if I shut my eyes.
How the exam asks it. Trim relieves pressure. Flaps add lift and drag. Spoilers kill lift. Know which does which.

The body's the fuselage. Crew, cargo, fuel in a lot of them. Wings come off it. The tail end is the empennage. Vertical stabilizer and rudder, horizontal stabilizer and elevator, and the trim tabs riding along. Up front, or out on the wings, the powerplant. That's the engine, a prop if it has one, and the cowling, the cover you unlatch to get at the engine, shaped to cut the wind and steer cooling air through. An engine hung out on a wing sits in a pod, the nacelle. You've had your head in four of those more times than I've had breakfast.

Landing gear comes two ways. Tricycle is two mains and a nose wheel, and that's most of what flies now. Conventional is two mains up front and a little wheel under the tail. Taildragger. They ground loop easy, and they sit nose high, so the pilot can't see a thing straight ahead on the ground and zigzags down the taxiway like a dog after a smell. Gear's fixed, hanging out in the wind all the time, or retractable, folding up out of it. Two two eight's folds up. You'd know what it weighs. I'd only guess.

A little piston engine has two magnetos making the spark. They run off the engine turning, not the battery, so the engine keeps going if the electrics die, and with two, one can quit and you're fine. The mixture sets how much fuel goes in with the air. Climb, and the air thins, so you lean it out or it runs rich and fouls the plugs. A carburetor can ice up inside on a cool damp morning with nothing in the sky, and on a fixed pitch prop the first you know is the rpm sagging. Pull the carb heat. Our tanker had four fans and none of that, and a whole set of troubles of its own.
How the exam asks it. Empennage is the tail. Cowling covers the engine. An easy pair to mix up.

I'll be quick, since I've only been up in one the once. A helicopter wears its wing over its head, going around. The main rotor. Every blade's an airfoil, same as ours, only spinning. Tip the whole spinning disc and part of the lift leans with it, forward or back or sideways, whichever way you tipped. That's all the getting around there is to it. No prop. People ask me that at the heritage room about once a month.

Three controls and a throttle. The collective's in the left hand, a lever like the parking brake in my dad's old Ford. Pull it up and every main blade takes a bigger bite at once, the same amount, and up she goes. Push it down, less bite, down she comes. Plenty of them have the throttle as a twist grip on the end of it, like a motorcycle, and a governor holds the rotor speed so the pilot can quit fretting about it. The cyclic's the stick between the knees, right hand. It tips the disc by giving each blade a little more bite on one side of the circle than the other, and the machine goes where the stick goes. The pedals are the feet, and they run the tail rotor.

The tail rotor's there on account of torque. Turn a big rotor one way and the body under it wants to go around the other way, Newton's third law, the same one that shoved me off the pool wall at the Y. The little rotor on the tail pushes sideways against it. More pedal, more push, and in a hover that's how the pilot swings the nose. If the engine quits, down goes the collective, and the air rushing up through the rotor as it sinks keeps the blades turning. Maple seed in May. Autorotation. Near the ground, collective back up, and the spin saved up in those blades sets it down soft. My one ride was over the Missouri in the flood of '93, in a Guard helicopter, and I held the seat frame the whole hour and didn't say a word.
How the exam asks it. Collective is up and down. Cyclic is which way. Pedals are the tail rotor.
Six gauges in front of a pilot in a little airplane, Sergeant. Three of them run on air. Three of them spin.

The air three hang off two holes. The pitot tube sticks out into the wind and catches it, ram air. The static port sits flush on the side of the fuselage and just feels the still pressure around the airplane. The airspeed indicator needs both. It reads the ram against the static, and that's your speed through the air. Altimeter and vertical speed indicator, static only. The altimeter reads how low the outside pressure's gotten and paints feet on it. The vertical speed indicator reads how fast that pressure's changing, in feet a minute. It gives you the trend right off. The number trails along six to nine seconds late.

The airspeed dial's got colored arcs. White is where you can run the flaps out, and its bottom end's the stall speed with flaps and gear down. Green's the normal range, and its bottom end is the stall speed clean. Yellow is caution, smooth air only. The red line at the end is never exceed. It means it.

The altimeter's got a little window you set to the altimeter setting the tower gives you. Set it on the ground and it ought to read the field's elevation above sea level, about. Fly from high pressure toward low without resetting, and it reads higher than you are. Same going from warm air into cold. High to low, or hot to cold, look out below. What it reads is indicated altitude. True altitude's your real height above sea level. Absolute's your height over the ground right under you. Pressure altitude's what it reads set to 29.92. Density altitude is pressure altitude fixed for temperature, and that's the one the wing and the engine feel in their bones. Standard day at sea level is 29.92 inches and 15 Celsius, a day I don't believe I've ever seen.
How the exam asks it. Static only, altimeter and VSI. Pitot and static, airspeed. That pair is worth knowing cold.

The three that spin are gyros. A spinning wheel holds its place in space and won't tip unless something leans on it. The attitude indicator's built on that. The gyro holds level while the airplane rolls and pitches around it. The heading indicator is a gyro too, a compass card that doesn't slosh around in the bumps. Every gyro drifts a little, though, so the pilot sets the heading indicator off the magnetic compass about every fifteen minutes. We had a pilot who did it every ten and wrote down every one.

The turn coordinator shows how fast you're rolling and turning. With its little airplane's wing on the mark, you're in a standard rate turn, three degrees a second, all the way around in two minutes. The ball underneath, in a curved tube of fluid, says whether the turn's coordinated. Ball off to one side, step on the rudder that side. Step on the ball, the instructors say, all of them, every one, like a church response.

The magnetic compass is a magnet floating in fluid, and it's got habits. It points at magnetic north, not true north, and the gap is variation. The airplane's own metal and wiring pull on it some, and that's deviation, written on a little card by the compass. Up here, heading east or west, speed up and it swings north, slow down and it swings south. Turning off north it lags behind, and off south it runs ahead. So pilots turn by the heading indicator and set it from the compass flying straight and steady. Ours was a whiskey compass. I told you that one. Every airplane I know still carries one, up on the glare shield, for the day everything else quits.
How the exam asks it. Heading indicator drifts, so it's set from the compass. Compass swings in turns, so you turn by the heading indicator.

A runway number is its magnetic heading, rounded to the nearest ten, last zero knocked off. Lined up on runway 31, you're pointed about 310, northwest. Lined up on 4, about 040. The other end of the same strip's 180 off, so add or take away 18 from the number. Runway 31's far end is 13. Parallel runways get letters. From the approach end, the left one's L and the right one's R, and a third one between them is C. Tolliver's alternate is 17 and 35. One strip, two names, and one NOTAM you've already read.

Runway markings are white. Taxiway paint is yellow. That one fact is worth the whole page. On the runway, the big number at the end, a dashed centerline, piano keys across the threshold, and about a thousand feet down, two fat white blocks, the aiming point. White arrows down the middle leading up to a white bar mean a displaced threshold. You can take off on the arrows and roll out onto them landing the other way, but you don't touch down there. Yellow chevrons ahead of the end mean a blast pad or overrun. Stay off it. A big yellow X says the runway's closed, and I'd believe it.

Where a taxiway runs into a runway there's a hold short line. Four yellow lines across the taxiway, two solid and two dashed. The solid ones face the side you're waiting on. Taxiing toward the runway, you stop before the solid lines, and you don't cross without a clearance from the control tower. Coming off the runway, you aren't clear of it till you've crossed the whole marking, dashed side first. A Cessna crossed one at Kansas City Downtown one night in 1991 without asking, and I heard the tower controller from two radios away.
How the exam asks it. White paint, runway. Yellow paint, taxiway. Stop on the solid side of a hold line.

Airport signs tell you what kind they are by color, before you've read a word, and on a dark ramp at four in the morning the color's the part you can make out. Red with white letters is an order. A runway holding position sign, with the runway's numbers on it, stands right at the hold line. Red can also be no entry, or the hold point for an ILS critical area. Black with yellow letters and a yellow border tells you where you are, the taxiway under you. Yellow with black letters and an arrow tells you which way. Black with a big white number along the runway's edge, that's thousands of feet you've got left.

Airport lighting at night. Runway edges are white. On a runway built for instrument approaches, the last two thousand feet go yellow, or the last half if the runway's short, so you know you're running out. Green across the near end, the threshold. Red across the far end. Taxiway edges are blue, taxiway centerlines green. Runway centerline's white, then red and white mixed for the last three thousand feet, then all red for the last thousand. Beside the touchdown point, the slope lights. On a PAPI, four in a row, two white and two red is right on the glidepath. More white, high. More red, low. The old two bar VASI says it in a rhyme. Red over white, you're all right. I've heard grown men sing it on final.

A wind sock points where the wind's going, so it's blowing in the big end. Standing straight out, call it fifteen knots or better. Radio dead? The control tower can talk to you with a light gun. In the air, steady green is cleared to land, flashing green is come back around to land, steady red is give way and keep circling, flashing red is the airport's no good, don't land. On the ground, flashing green, cleared to taxi. Steady green, cleared for takeoff. Steady red, stop. Flashing red, get off the runway. Flashing white, go back where you started. Red and green taking turns, be very careful, anywhere. I saw a light gun used for real exactly once, at Whiteman, and the pilot it was pointed at landed like he was carrying eggs.
How the exam asks it. Red sign's an order. Blue light's a taxiway. All red on a PAPI means you're low, and lower if you wait.
The pattern, right of way, and the gate.

An airport without a tower still has a shape to it, the traffic pattern. A box around the runway, usually flown with left turns, about a thousand feet over the ground. Off the runway on the departure leg. Turn onto crosswind, then downwind, running alongside the runway the opposite way from landing. Then base, then final, lined up on the runway. You join it on a 45 degree angle to downwind, about halfway along. A segmented circle out by the wind sock tells you if the pattern runs right hand instead.

Right of way, mostly common sense, with a few you'd never guess. An aircraft in distress goes first, ahead of everybody. Two coming together from the side, the one on the right has it. Head on, both turn right. Overtaking, you pass on their right, and they've got the right of way. Landing traffic goes ahead of traffic in the air, and of two coming in, the lower one goes first, though it can't cut in. Balloons have it over everything, then gliders. And here's my favorite. An aircraft refueling another one has right of way over every other powered aircraft in the sky, airships included. That was us. Best rule in the book.

Airport security. An airport with airlines draws a secured area, and a military flight line does the same, with a red line painted on the ramp you don't step over without a reason. The rules look alike most places. Badge on, where it shows. Nobody follows you through a gate or a door on your badge. Somebody inside with no badge, you stop them and ask, or call it in, whichever your airport says. Somebody on escort stays with whoever's escorting them. I wore a badge on a lanyard thirty one years at the freight terminal, and the one morning I left it in the car, a nineteen year old guard I'd watched grow up made me walk back for it in the sleet. He was right, and I told him so.
How the exam asks it. Downwind is the leg flown alongside the runway, the opposite way from landing. Left turns unless the airport says right.

At twenty past four she and Fisk walked two two eight with their flashlights, nose to tail, the way they did every launch. He'd brought her a coffee from the machine, which he did now on drill mornings without saying why.
He'd slept. She could tell from how he walked, and from his eyes, and from the fact that he'd remembered both gloves. He didn't say how, and she didn't ask.

Under the left wing he stopped and put his light on the leading edge, the long rounded front of it, wet with dew. Boom operator told me Thursday a wing can stall with its nose pointed straight at the ground. I told him that's when you've got the most speed. He said look it up, Airman. I didn't look it up.
Fisk wants to know who's right. What does Kit tell him?
A. Not likely. Nose down means speed, and speed keeps a wing flying.
B. Only if there's ice on the wing. The boom means winter.
C. He's right. It's the wing's angle to the air, not to the ground.
D. No. A stall is when the engines quit, so the nose has nothing to do with it.

She put her own light up beside his. It's the angle to the air, she told him. Tip the front of a wing up into the air coming at it far enough, and the air can't stay on top. It lets go, and the lift goes with it. Nose high, nose low, fast or slow. Pull hard out of a dive and you can get there with the nose pointed at a cornfield. Fisk stood with his light on the wing like it might do it right then. Guess I owe him a coffee. Two. He's a boom operator.

That'll hold, Sergeant. That's it, the critical angle of attack, measured against the relative wind. Every wing has one, and past it the air peels off the top and the lift falls away. Where the nose points doesn't decide it, and the speed doesn't by itself either. So any attitude, any airspeed, any power setting. The fix is less angle. My first year on tankers a boom operator told me the same thing, and I argued with him too, and it cost me a dollar.
Two two eight came off the ground at eight thirty one and turned out over the river. Kit watched it until it was a dot, then walked to the office.

Boyd had a launch sheet in one hand and his cup in the other. The picture of him at twenty by the nose gear was still taped to the side of his monitor, curling at the corners. She shut the door behind her. He looked at it, and then at her.
That's twice this year you've shut my door, Darrow. He set the cup down on the inbox, where the routing slip had sat for almost four weeks in January. Go ahead.
Boyd's waiting, and he's a busy man. How should Kit start?
A. Start with what the package needs from him, and work around to 2019.
B. Thank him for all of 2019, and then tell him the truth.
C. Say the score first, plainly, before anything else.
D. Tell him Graham and Vern both know already so he ought to hear it too.

It wasn't the inspection, Sergeant Boyd. My Pilot score came back nineteen that fall, and it has to be twenty five. You asked me to stay, and I said yes so I'd never have to say nineteen on this ramp. Every time a board went up and you looked at me like you owed me, I let you pay. She didn't sit down. She didn't take the sheet out of her coat. She said it standing up, the way you'd report a write up.

Right. Log it. Integrity, and Communication. You put the fact at the front, in your own words, with nothing stacked ahead of it. You didn't make him wait through a speech to find out what he's being told. Hard news to the person it most concerns, privately and plainly, is where the key leans. He's the one who's been paying on it. He gets it first from you, standing up.

For a while Boyd didn't say anything. He picked up the cup and didn't drink from it. Then he laughed, once, through his nose, and put his hand flat over his eyes, the way a man does when the bill he's been paying turns out to be somebody else's.
Seven years. Every time a board went up on that corkboard, I'd look at you and think, there's the one I cost. And you let me.

He put the cup down. You want to know why your slip sat under that cup? When these jets go, I go. Thirty one years on this airplane. I built you to stay. You were the one thing on this ramp I wasn't going to have to hand back.
And DARROW on every launch? Both. Keeping you close. And putting you in front of her every Saturday so she'd see what she'd be getting.
He's mad, and he's told her why he held on. What does Kit say?
A. Promise him that if the board says no, she'll stay and run the shop.
B. Tell him she'll have Fisk ready to run two two eight before she leaves.
C. Tell him the package is past him now, and it's the colonel's call.
D. Tell him she's sorry he carried it, and that she still wants to go.

I'm sorry you carried it. I let you. And I still want to go. Boyd looked at her for a long time, long enough for the phone on his desk to ring and quit. Yeah. I know you do. That's the part I'm mad about. He picked up the launch sheet again. Go on. Your jet's back at one.

That's the fix I'd have taken. You owned what you did, said what you want, and didn't trade one against the other. You didn't argue with his anger, and you didn't try to buy it off. On the test, the action that takes responsibility and stays honest about the goal usually beats the one that makes everybody comfortable. Integrity, with Communication right behind it.
At a quarter to twelve she walked to the heritage room on her lunch. Vern was at the slate table with a paper sack and a thermos. He looked up.

She sat down across from him and didn't say anything. He looked at her a while. Then he got up, took the keys off his belt, and got the case open on the first try this time. Out from under the glass came the attitude indicator. Corbin's altimeter stayed put, its needles on field elevation. The old dial went on the table between them. A crack in the glass at seven o'clock, and a little white airplane painted across the middle.

It's dead. No gyro spinning in there, so the card just hangs where it falls. That's fine. I'll draw you the live one. He went to the slate board on the wall, the one older than he was, and drew with a stub of chalk out of his shirt pocket. A circle. A little airplane across the middle with its wings straight out. Then the horizon line, sky over it and ground under. The line went up over the little airplane, uphill to the right. The grade on the river road, about.
Line above the little airplane, higher on the right. What is it doing?

Two looks. Line over the nose. Nose down. Diving. Wings next. Uphill to the right meant the right end was the high end. Right wing low. Banked right. Vern rubbed it out with the side of his fist and drew another before she could feel good about it.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Pitch first, then bank. Horizon over the little airplane, nose under it, diving. For the bank, look at which end of the line is higher. Line's high on the right, so the right wing's the low one. Right bank, and on a real dial the pointer would sit off zero to the right to back you up. That took you about six seconds. You'd have had six to spare, and you'll want them for the ones that point at you.
On the shelf by the case was a gray desk model of a tanker on a stand, missing its boom, with a tag on it in Patrice's printing that said PLEASE DO NOT HANDLE. Vern handled it.
On the test you're always standing south of it, at its height, looking north. I'm north. East is your right. He held the model out across the table at his eye level, nose pointed straight at her.
Then he tipped it. The wing on her left side went down, the wing on her right came up. Nose still at her, level.
Heading and bank, Sergeant. Twelve seconds.
Nose toward her, the wing on her left dipped. What's the model doing?
C. Heading east, and banked right.

Nose at her, so south. Then she put herself in the seat, facing her own chair. From in there, the low wing was on the right hand. Banked right. Vern set the model back on its stand, nose to the wall, the way Patrice liked it.

Right. Log it. Nose toward you is heading south. Then sit in the seat. Facing you, the airplane's right wing is on your left, so a dip on your left is a right bank. That's the one people miss most, and the test knows it. Slow down on the nose toward you pictures. They're worth the extra two seconds.
At twenty past twelve she put her coat back on. Vern was screwing the lid onto his thermos.

She'd said one thing this morning she'd held for seven years. This one she'd held since January, at a diner counter, where she'd nearly asked him and hadn't. She'd sat at his kitchen table every Tuesday since, with a box in the den with 2001 on the end of it, and hadn't. She'd been seven that summer.
She knew three things about family day. A navigator's seat, too big for her. A man's voice. A hand pointing up at the ceiling. She didn't know which jet, and she didn't know the man's face.
She stood by the case with her coat on and looked up at the ceiling tiles, which had nothing in them.
She's never asked him. How does Kit bring it up?
A. Leave it, and ask her mother about the picture first.
B. Ask Patrice on Tuesday, so he isn't put on the spot.
C. Ask him straight if he was on family day in 2001.
D. Ask if he's got a June 2001 log she could study this week.

Were you on family day in 2001? I sat in a navigator's seat that summer. I was seven. I don't know whose jet it was. Vern set the thermos down. He held still the way he did when the egg timer was about to go, and it wasn't anywhere near going. June. We had one that June. He looked at the case, not at her. It's in the box. It's the one I haven't picked. I'll bring it tomorrow.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Communication. You asked the person who'd know, directly, in your own words, and you said why it mattered to you. You didn't dress it up as homework or send the question around through somebody else. That's the key's lean on any question you're afraid of the answer to.

She thought about June on the walk back and made herself stop. Two two eight came home at ten past one. Kit and Fisk drove out to meet it in the truck, the long way around on the perimeter road, because the short way crossed the alternate runway and nobody had called the tower for it.

The road ran beside a taxiway for a stretch. Where the taxiway met the alternate runway there were four yellow lines across the concrete, two solid and two dashed, and beside them a sign on two little legs. Red, with white numbers on it, 17-35.
I drive past that every drill. Red means stop, I figure, and then you just go?
What should Kit tell Fisk the red sign means?
A. It tells you where you are, the way a street sign does.
B. It marks a taxiway that's closed to traffic for the weekend.
C. Stop, look both ways, and go if it's clear.
D. It's an order: runway ahead, and nobody crosses without the tower.

Red with white letters was an order, she told him. A runway holding position sign. The runway's just past it, 17 at one end and 35 at the other, and you don't put a tire over the solid lines till the tower says so. Truck or airplane, same rule. Fisk turned in his seat to watch it go by. So, stop and wait. Not stop and go. He said it again under his breath, the way he'd say a torque value.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Red with white lettering is a mandatory sign. This one's a runway holding position sign, with the runway's numbers on it, right at the hold line. Stop on the solid side of those four lines and don't cross without a clearance. Black with yellow letters tells you where you are. Yellow with black letters and an arrow says which way to go. You know what kind of sign it is from the color before you've read a word, and on a dark ramp in the rain the color's what you can see.

At three there was an engine run. Number two had come home with a write up on its oil pressure, a flicker in the climb, and the specialists wanted it run at power once they'd been through it. Kit took the left seat. Fisk was on the long interphone cord out by the engine, where he could see it.

She ran the checklist the way she'd run it a hundred times, brakes set, chocks in, clearance from the tower on the radio. Number two came up to power, and the jet leaned into the chocks and stayed put.

Then, with the gauges steady and nothing to do but watch them, she did something she'd never done in eleven years in that seat. She looked at the rest of the panel the way a pilot would. The attitude display in front of her, the little airplane sitting on the horizon line, wings level, nose a hair above, the way the jet sat on its gear on this end of the ramp. Level flight, if it had been flying. The heading read 320. Northwest and a little more. The direction she'd be pointed, if anybody ever let her off these brakes. At eight thirty one, two two eight had gone off the end of this runway and turned right for the river, out to 050. Vern had sat sideways behind that turn for twenty years and never once seen it from here.
She thought of Vern's card from the lesson, three degrees a second, all the way around in two minutes.
From 320, around to the right to 050, at standard rate. How long does it take?
A. Thirty seconds. That's a 90 degree turn at 3 a second.
B. Four and a half minutes. 270 degrees, at 1 a second each.
C. Ninety seconds. That's the 270 degrees going left.
D. Ninety seconds, a second for every degree.

Forty degrees from 320 up to north. Fifty more past north to 050. Ninety, all told. At three degrees a second that was thirty seconds. She had it before number two's oil pressure needle had moved. Then the specialist's voice came over the interphone, asking for idle, and she brought it back.

Right. Log it. Count the turn in two pieces when it crosses north. From 320 to 360 is 40, and from 000 to 050 is 50, so 90 in all. At three degrees a second, 90 divided by 3 is thirty seconds. Same answer as a quarter of the two minute circle. The miss is subtracting the headings straight, 320 less 50, and turning the long way.
Saturday night Graham had been at the kitchen table with a pack of blank index cards and his black marker. When she came in he turned the stack face down and asked how Boyd took it.

Sunday at seven a medevac helicopter came in low over the river and set down on the pad on the civil side, by the terminal. A white van was already there with its back doors open, and two people in blue stood well off to one side holding their caps on. Fisk stopped with a tow bar in his hands. The helicopter hung there a few feet up with its nose down a little, and the grass along the pad went flat and silver. Then it slid forward across the concrete, with nothing pushing it either of them could see, and sat down.
Fisk watched the blades wind down. Kemp says if you get it you're gone a year, easy. Who's on her then? Kit didn't answer that one. It wasn't hers to answer yet. He looked back at the pad.
How's it go forward? There's no prop.
No prop on it, and it moved off forward. Which control did that?
A. The cyclic. It tips the rotor, and the lift pulls it along.
B. The pedals. They swing the tail rotor around to push it.
C. The collective. More pitch on the blades, and it goes.
D. The tail rotor. It turns back, and it works like a prop.

She'd seen the nose dip before it went. The stick. Cyclic. He leans it, the whole spinning thing up top leans with it, and some of the lift pulls him forward. Fisk chewed on that, tow bar still in his hands. Like leaning into a walk. Close enough for a Sunday.

That's the fix I'd have taken. The cyclic. Lean the stick and the rotor disc leans, because each blade takes a little more bite on one side of the circle than the other. Leaned forward, part of the lift pulls forward. The collective's up and down. The pedals point the nose. I learned that hollering back and forth with a Guard pilot over the river in '93. I caught about half of what he said, and that half was the cyclic.
Decision ten. The one he hadn't picked.
At noon he was at the slate table again, with no sack and no thermos. He had a log in front of him, folded once and squared to the edge of the table.
He'd said he'd bring it. He slid it across to her and kept two fingers on it a second before he let go.
She unfolded it. His capitals, the same square hand as every other one, a little bigger, as if he'd been writing it on his knee.

Nine June, oh one. Family day. Two two eight on static, north ramp. Nav seat open ten to fifteen hundred. Thirty some kids. One girl about seven would not get out. Asked what the hole in the ceiling is for. Told her that's where the stars come in. Asked me which seat is the best one. Told her this one. She did not believe me.
Two two eight. She read it again. She looked up, and he was looking at the case, the way he had yesterday.
He's asked her plainly, and he's waiting. What does Kit answer?
A. Tell him yes, it was her. It had to be.
B. Say she doesn't know yet, and she'll call him from her mother's.
C. Say it could've been anybody. There were thirty kids that day.
D. Tell him she'll bring the picture to his table on Tuesday.

I don't know yet. My mother's got a picture on her fridge from that day. I'll know by supper, and I'll call you either way. Vern nodded once. He refolded the log along its old crease and pushed it back across to her. Keep it on you. She put it in her coat, on top of everything else in there.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Integrity and Communication, both. You told him what you know and what you don't, and you didn't give him a yes you couldn't stand behind. You put a time on the rest, today, and said you'd call either way. That's how you'd close any loop on a flight line. It works on a man in a heritage room too.
At half past three, with the shop half closed down for release, Boyd called her into his office. The door was already shut when she got there. He opened it for her and shut it again.

There was a yellow legal pad on the desk, one page written on in pencil, in the square printing he'd used on her training records when she was twenty one. The pencil was a carpenter's pencil, flat, sharpened on the bench grinder. She'd never seen him write anything longer than a forms entry.

For your package. I did it at my kitchen table last night. My wife says it's fine. She'd say that. He put one thick finger on a word near the bottom. Before I read it to you. You're the one studying words. I wrote that I recommend you unequivocally. Does that mean what I think it means?
UNEQUIVOCALLY: closest in meaning. What does Kit tell him?
A. Equally, the same as everybody else.
B. Without any doubt or hedge.
C. Strongly, with real feeling behind it.
D. Loudly, so the whole board hears it.
It means no doubt in it. No but. Boyd nodded slowly, the way he did when a torque value came out where he'd expected. Then it stays.

Right. Log it. Unequivocally. Plainly, with no doubt and no hedge. Equivocal means it could go either way, a word that speaks with two voices. Put un in front and it can't. Whatever else is on the page, the closest choice is the one with no doubt in it.
He read it to her once, standing at the desk, the pad held out at arm's length because he wouldn't wear his glasses in front of her. Halfway into the first line he stopped and looked up.
Look at me, Darrow. Not the floor. She looked at him, and he read the rest of it to her face.

To the selection board. I have been on the KC-135 since 1996, and I have been Staff Sergeant Katherine Darrow's supervisor since she was twenty one. She is the best crew chief I have trained. In March she held a jet the forms said was ready, and she was right. She tells the truth when it costs her. That is the thing I would want in the seat. I recommend her unequivocally. Seven years ago I asked her to stay, and she did. I am not asking again. Arlen Boyd, Master Sergeant.

He signed it with the carpenter's pencil, pressed hard enough to go through, the way he'd signed her slip. He tore it off the pad. Then he said the other thing to the window. Your name stays under that window till you fly it. If the new jets come first, I'll paint it on one of them myself.
Vern had told her in February that the board could get that one from Boyd.
At ten after four she pulled up at her mother's across the river. Rhonda had the roast on, and the kitchen windows were steamed, and she'd set two places at the table where Kit had done her homework.

They ate first. Then Kit put her fork down and told her. The nineteen. The yes. Boyd, yesterday, with his door shut. The letter, an hour ago. Rhonda listened with her hands around her coffee, and when it was over she said Kitty, once. I've been bragging on a girl who stayed for her people. I'll brag on this one now. You can argue with me about it some other night.
The family day picture was where it had been since 2001, on the freezer door, under the dentist magnet. April's lunch menu was clipped over the top half. Taco Tuesday. Kit got up and unclipped it.

She was seven in it, in a seat too big for her, in a green T shirt, looking up. A man's arm came in from the edge of the picture, cut off at the shoulder by her mother's camera, and his hand pointed at a small round fitting in the ceiling. On the hand was a ring. Gold, with a stone, worn thin on one side. She'd shaken that hand at the Riverside in January.

Her mother watched her from the sink. You cried from the gate to the bridge that day. I asked what hurt, and you said nothing hurt. You said you wanted to go back and sit in it. She dried her hands on the towel. I never did get that man's name.
It's her mother's picture, on her mother's fridge. What does Kit do with it?
A. Tell her mother it ought to go to Vern, since it's his hand.
B. Clip the menu back over it and leave it where it's always been.
C. Take a picture of it with her phone and send it to Vern now.
D. Ask her mother if she can keep it.

Mom. Can I have this? I want it. She heard herself say it. Not for Vern. Not for the board. Rhonda looked at the picture in her hand, then at her. Kitty, it's been yours since you were seven. I was just keeping it on the fridge. Then Kit told her whose hand that was. Vern Pruett. He was the navigator. He's the one teaching me.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity, the plainest kind, and the hardest one for you. You asked for something you want, for yourself, in your own words, and you didn't hang a reason on it for anybody else. It's her picture, so you asked. You didn't take. On the test and off it, the key leans toward the direct ask over the clever workaround.

After the dishes she took her phone out on the back step, the one with the crack she'd put in it on roller skates in third grade, and called him. He picked up on the first ring, the way her mother did, and didn't bother with hello.
It was me. In your seat. Your ring's in the picture.
Nothing on the line a while but his television down the hall, the Royals, and Patrice telling the umpire what she thought. Then he cleared his throat.
Keep it that way, Sergeant. He hung up before she could think what to say back. She sat a minute longer with the phone in her lap, listening to a car go over the bridge.

Inside, her mother had wrapped half the roast in foil for Graham and written on it in cafeteria marker, GRAHAM, 350, 20 MIN, as if he'd never warmed up a roast in his life. The picture lay face up by her cup.

Her mother went in the drawer by the stove for a quart freezer bag. In went the picture. Out went the air, the way she did the buns on Fridays. She zipped it. Then she handed it across. Seven years old. Green shirt. Too big a seat. Looking up. She didn't put it in her coat. She carried it out to the truck in her hand, the way you'd carry something you meant to show somebody.
